teaser: He is supposed to be all mind. So why did Rodin give him the body of a wrestler?
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo shows an outdoor bronze cast in front of a modern office building (a bank sign is visible), seen from the figure's left side and slightly behind. It is not the Musee Rodin cast in Paris. Spots describe only what this view shows.
Original figure about 70 cm, designed around 1880 for The Gates of Hell; enlarged version about 1.9 m, shown in 1904; enlargement carried out by Henri Lebosse.
Bronze installed in front of the Pantheon in 1906 after a public subscription, moved to the Musee Rodin in 1922.
Rodin's statement that the figure thinks with every muscle, clenched fist and gripping toes: well-known quote, paraphrased here.
Name 'The Thinker' attributed to foundry workers noticing the likeness to Michelangelo's seated Lorenzo de' Medici ('Il Penseroso').
Cleveland Museum of Art cast damaged by a bomb in March 1970 and left unrepaired.
More than twenty full-size bronze casts worldwide.

lesson.text: Thinking is the quietest thing a person can do. It needs no strength at all. Yet the most famous image of thought ever made is a naked giant with a furrowed back and thighs like tree trunks, who looks as if he could lift the rock he sits on. Something here does not add up, and Rodin meant it that way.

The figure began small and with another job. Around 1880, Auguste Rodin was asked to make monumental bronze doors for a museum in Paris. He chose the subject himself: the Inferno of Dante, the medieval Italian poem about a journey through hell. The doors became known as The Gates of Hell.

At the top of the doors, above the swarm of the damned, Rodin seated a man about 70 centimeters high (28 inches). He called him The Poet. This was Dante, looking down at the world he was inventing. Not a spectator of hell, but its author.

The name we use came from the workshop. Foundry workers reportedly nicknamed the figure “the Thinker” because it reminded them of a brooding seated statue by Michelangelo known by that name in Italian.

A poet from the 1300s would normally wear a long robe and a laurel wreath. Rodin stripped all of that away. Without clothes there is no century and no profession left, only a man. He wanted a body that could stand for anyone who has ever struggled with an idea.

So how do you make thought visible, when it happens where no one can see? Rodin's answer was to treat it as labor. He once explained that his figure thinks not just with his brain but with every muscle of his arms, back and legs. The pose shows how.
This photo catches him from the side and a little behind. Trace how the body folds.

lines.label: The bowed back
lines.text: From skull to seat, one long curve. The spine bends like a bow under load, and the ridged muscles along it are working, not resting.

lines.label: The near arm
lines.text: The arm on our side drops to the knee and the hand hangs loose. Behind it, the other arm crosses the body to prop up the chin: a twist no one holds for long in comfort.

lines.label: Down to the toes
lines.text: Thigh, shin and foot zigzag back under the body. Head, arms and legs all turn inward. Nothing in him opens toward the outside world.

lesson.text: Try the pose yourself: right elbow on the left knee, chin on the back of the hand. Your torso twists and your stomach tightens within seconds. Rodin picked a position that is uncomfortable on purpose. This man is not daydreaming. He is in the middle of an effort.
Rodin said the figure thinks even with the part of the body farthest from his head. Can you find where the tension ends up?

spots.title: The gripping toes
spots.text: His toes curl down and clutch the edge of the rock. Even here, as far from the brain as a body gets, nothing is relaxed.

lesson.text: In 1904 Rodin had the little poet enlarged to about 1.9 meters (over 6 feet) and showed him alone, cut loose from the doors. On its own the figure changed meaning. Dante disappeared, and what remained was a monument to thinking itself.

The enlargement was not carved or remodeled by hand from scratch. A specialist, Henri Lebossé, scaled up Rodin's sculptures using a mechanical device that copies a form point by point at a larger size.

Parisians paid for a bronze cast through a public collection, and in 1906 it was set in front of the Panthéon, the building where France buries its great men. It was moved in 1922 to the Musée Rodin. More than twenty other full-size casts now sit around the world, including the one in this photograph.

That is a peculiarity of bronze. The sculptor models in clay, a mold is taken, and molten metal can be poured into it again and again. Each cast is an original in the eyes of the law and of museums, so The Thinker can be in Paris, Tokyo and outside an office block at once.
In 1970 a bomb was set off under the cast outside the Cleveland Museum of Art, tearing open its base and legs. The museum chose not to repair it and still displays the damaged figure.

Rodin died in 1917 and is buried in Meudon, outside Paris. Over the grave sits a cast of The Thinker, placed there at his own wish. The man who started as Dante watching over hell ended as Rodin's headstone.
Rodin showed thinking as something the whole body does. The muscles are not a contradiction of the mind: they are his way of making an invisible effort visible.

quiz.question: What was the figure first called?
quiz.explanation: Rodin named him The Poet, meaning Dante above The Gates of Hell.

quiz.question: Why did Rodin leave the figure nude?
options: He ran out of time to add clothes
So he would belong to no period and could stand for anyone
quiz.explanation: Without a robe or wreath, he is simply a man struggling with an idea.

quiz.question: What do the figure's toes do?
quiz.explanation: The toes curl and clutch the rock, tense like the rest of the body.

quiz.question: Where was the large bronze first installed in Paris in 1906?
options: On top of The Gates of Hell
quiz.explanation: It stood before the Panthéon until it moved to the Musée Rodin in 1922.

quiz.question: Why can The Thinker be seen in many cities at once?
options: Bronze can be cast several times from a mold
Rodin carved many copies in marble
Most of them are plastic replicas
quiz.explanation: Molten bronze can be poured into the mold again and again.

facts.text: The Thinker was originally about 70 centimeters high.
facts.explanation: The first version sat at the top of The Gates of Hell at roughly that size.

facts.text: The pose is a relaxed, comfortable one.
facts.explanation: Elbow on the opposite knee twists the torso: Rodin chose an effortful pose.

facts.text: A cast of The Thinker sits over Rodin's grave.
facts.explanation: He asked for one to be placed on his tomb in Meudon.
